Britain held large stockpiles from the bumper 1860 crop, and within a couple of seasons Egypt and India expanded planting enormously to fill the gap; Egypt's cotton boom under Khedive Ismail was financed by debt that ended, by a longer road, in British occupation in 1882. Meanwhile Britain depended on the Union for grain, and intervention risked war with the North, Canada, and its merchant fleet. So King Cotton's diplomacy failed on supply substitution — the classic fate of a resource weapon once buyers find other sources. The episode's longer shadow fell on Egypt and India, whose fields were permanently rearranged by a war fought an ocean away over a plant's geography.
Why would the Netherlands trade away New Amsterdam — modern New York — for a tiny island most people have never heard of?

Because in 1667 the tiny island was worth more. The island was Run, in the Banda group, and its wealth was nutmeg: in the seventeenth century nutmeg grew naturally almost nowhere else on Earth, and in Europe it sold at fantastic markups over its cost in the islands. The Treaty of Breda that year settled the Second Anglo-Dutch War with a swap in which England kept New Amsterdam, on the Hudson, and the Dutch secured their hold on Run and the Banda nutmeg monopoly — a trade that looked, to contemporaries, entirely rational. The episode is the purest illustration of how spice geography distorted values: a monopoly crop concentrated on a few volcanic specks could outweigh a harbour and a river system on another continent, because the price gradient across distance was so extreme — a shipload of spice could repay the cost of the voyage many times over, while North American furs and farms could not. Vasco da Gama's whole enterprise had been aimed at that gradient: reach the source by sea and cut out the chain of middlemen. When the gradient collapsed, so did the valuations — and Manhattan's side of the bargain began its long revenge.
Why did Britain and France treat tiny Caribbean sugar islands as prizes worth more than huge territories in Canada?

Because in the eighteenth century a sugar island was a money machine and Canada, in Voltaire's sneer, was a few acres of snow. The Caribbean formula combined tropical climate, sea transport on every side, and the labour of enslaved Africans to produce sugar — a high-value, non-perishable cargo — at profits no northern colony could match. Saint-Domingue, the western third of one island, produced on the order of a third of the world's sugar by the 1780s and was arguably the most valuable colony on Earth. At the peace table of 1763 Britain seriously weighed keeping Guadeloupe, a speck of sugar land, against keeping all of Canada, and took Canada largely for strategic reasons while returning the sugar island to France. Sugar also shaped war aims and naval strategy for a century: convoys, hurricane-season campaigning, and island-hopping expeditions all served the plantation economy. The valuations look insane only in hindsight. Measured in revenue per acre, the diplomats were right — the tragedy is that the revenue was built on slavery, which is precisely why the islands' profits and their violence were inseparable.
Why did Oregon Trail wagon trains all leave Missouri in the same few weeks of spring?

Because the trail had two deadlines and only one window satisfied both. Leave too early, in March, and there was no grass on the plains for the oxen — the train's engines would starve before reaching the mountains. Leave too late, and the Sierra Nevada or Cascades would be blocked by snow before the wagons arrived, as the Donner Party proved. So emigrants 'jumped off' in April and May, when the prairie grass could feed draft animals, for a journey of some 3,200 kilometres paced by grazing and water: daily marches ran from water source to water source along the Platte, the Snake, and the dry stretches between. The trail's whole rhythm — where camps formed, where graves accumulated, where cholera struck in the bad years of 1849 to 1852 — was set by forage, water spacing, and the snow line at the far end. Several hundred thousand people made the crossing over two decades, all of them passengers of the same calendar. Migration at wagon speed is a logistics operation, and its timetable is written by grass and weather.
What actually went wrong for the Donner Party in 1846?

A calendar failure, compounding. The party of emigrants bound for California left Illinois in April 1846 — already at the late edge of the safe window — and then, in July, chose to follow the Hastings Cutoff, an untested shortcut promoted by a man who had never taken wagons over it. The cutoff cost them weeks instead of saving them: hacking a track through the Wasatch mountains, then crossing some eighty miles of waterless salt desert, which killed oxen, destroyed wagons, and consumed the margin the season allowed. They reached the Sierra Nevada in late October just as an early storm closed the pass, and were trapped in the snow a few kilometres from the summit. Of roughly eighty-seven people who entered the mountains, about forty-eight survived the winter. The margin between the Donner Party's fame and an unremarkable crossing was about two weeks of schedule — spent on a shortcut that wasn't. Emigrant logistics ran on a simple equation: grass, water, and snow dates; the cutoff broke all three terms at once.
How did the Erie Canal make New York, rather than Philadelphia or New Orleans, the great port of the American interior?

By giving New York the only cheap route through the Appalachian wall. The canal, opened in 1825 along the Hudson–Mohawk corridor — the one water-level gap in the mountain chain — cut the cost of moving a ton of freight between Buffalo and New York City from roughly a hundred dollars to under ten, and the journey from about twenty days to under a week. The effect was to re-aim the trade of the entire Great Lakes and Ohio country: produce that had floated down the Mississippi to New Orleans, or crawled overland to Philadelphia and Baltimore, now flowed east through the canal to New York's docks, banks, and shipping lines. Philadelphia and Baltimore answered with railroads and canals of their own, but they were fighting topography — their routes had to climb. A canal is a machine for deleting distance, and the Erie deleted it so thoroughly that it rearranged the urban hierarchy of a continent: the port at the end of the easiest gradient won.
What did the Suez Canal actually change when it opened in 1869?

It deleted roughly half the ocean between Europe and Asia. The voyage from London to Bombay fell from about 19,500 kilometres around the Cape of Good Hope to about 10,700 through Suez — a saving of some two-fifths to a half, depending on the route measured. Two subtler changes mattered as much. First, the canal favoured steam over sail: sailing ships could not work the canal or the Red Sea's contrary winds effectively, so Suez accelerated the merchant world's conversion to steam and to the coaling-station networks steam required. Second, it converted Egypt into the jugular of the British Empire: Britain bought the Khedive's canal shares in 1875 and occupied Egypt in 1882, and imperial strategy from Gibraltar to Aden reorganized itself around keeping that ditch open. A hundred and ninety kilometres of excavated desert re-sorted the trade, the navies, and the politics of three continents — the clearest proof that distance in economics is not measured in kilometres but in cost and time, and both can be edited.
Why was Russia's Trans-Siberian Railway a strategic weakness in the war with Japan in 1904–05, even though it connected Moscow to the Pacific?

Because a connection is not a capacity. The line to Vladivostok and the Manchurian front was single-track: trains could only pass each other at station loops, which capped throughput at a handful of train pairs a day, and until the Circum-Baikal section was finished, trains were even ferried across Lake Baikal — in winter, over rails laid on the ice. Russia's army in Manchuria therefore sat at the end of some nine thousand kilometres of the thinnest possible supply line, and reinforcements, guns, and shells arrived at the pace the loops allowed. Japan, by contrast, supplied its armies by sea over short distances from home ports, and could concentrate force faster than Russia could feed it across a continent. The war became a contest between a railway timetable and a sea lane, and the sea lane won — Russia's defeat owed as much to passing-loop spacing as to Japanese generalship. The lesson generalizes painfully: on a map, a line looks like a capability. In logistics, only the tonnage per day is real.
How did Polynesian voyagers manage to settle islands scattered across the largest ocean on Earth without maps or instruments?

By treating the voyage itself as a supply and navigation system. The settlement of the Pacific triangle — Hawaii, Rapa Nui, and New Zealand, the last reached by roughly the thirteenth century — was done in large double-hulled canoes that were freight carriers as much as boats: they carried colonists, breeding animals, and the cuttings and seeds of taro, yam, banana, and breadfruit, a portable farm that had to survive weeks at sea, along with water in gourds and bamboo and preserved foods. Navigation ran on memorized star paths, the direction of ocean swells, and the flight ranges of land-based birds. Evidence for deliberate two-way voyaging, and for contact with South America — the sweet potato, an American plant, was established in Polynesia before Europeans arrived — suggests these were return-capable expeditions, not accidental drifts. Each successful landfall then had to solve the island's own logistics: fresh water, reef resources, and soil for the transported crops. The Pacific was settled by the best pre-modern logistics system ever built for open ocean.
Why did the Allied advance across the Pacific in World War II move in jumps between particular islands instead of just pushing forward?

Because the jumps were measured in fighter range. Land-based aircraft could only escort shipping and cover landings within a few hundred kilometres of an airfield, so the advance had to proceed airfield by airfield: seize an island, build or repair a strip — the Seabees sometimes had planes operating within days — and the next objective had to lie within that umbrella. Islands that didn't fit the geometry could simply be bypassed: the great Japanese base at Rabaul was neutralized from the air and left to 'wither on the vine', its garrison of tens of thousands stranded by sea and air blockade, irrelevant to a war that had hopped past it. Each capture converted a stretch of open ocean into land-based air cover and a supply anchorage, shortening the effective distance to the next jump. The road from Guadalcanal to Okinawa looks on a map like a line of conquests; operationally it was a chain of airfields and harbours, spaced by aircraft range and shipping capacity. In the Pacific, geography was measured in runway lengths.
The Burke and Wills expedition crossed Australia in 1861 and then its leaders starved to death. What went wrong?

A rendezvous failed by hours. The Victorian expedition reached the Gulf of Carpentaria — the first European crossing of the continent south to north — but its survival plan depended on a depot at Cooper Creek, where a support party with supplies waited at a camp marked by a blaze on a coolibah tree, the famous Dig Tree. The depot party, having waited four months and believing the explorers dead, departed on the morning of 21 April 1861. Burke, Wills, and King, starving and exhausted, arrived that same evening — hours too late — and, fatally, the departing party left no clear signal on the blaze that they had gone that day, while Burke buried a note the depot party never found when they briefly returned. Burke and Wills died by the creek in the following weeks, despite food from local Aboriginal people; King alone survived. Expedition logistics in country that cannot feed you is a chain of timed rendezvous, and the chain's strength is measured in hours. The crossing was a triumph of endurance built on a scheduling system with no slack in it.
Why did the Norse settlements in Greenland die out after about four centuries?

The supply-line answer is strong but not the whole story, and honesty requires saying so. Greenland's Norse, settled from about 985, lived at the end of one of the world's longest and most dangerous supply lines, weeks of sailing from Norway via Iceland. They imported what the country could not provide — timber, iron, grain — and paid with exports, above all walrus ivory. When elephant ivory returned to European markets in quantity, Greenland ivory prices fell; shipping thinned; and the climate's slide into the Little Ice Age shortened the hay season the cattle economy depended on. The Western Settlement was gone by roughly the mid-1300s and the Eastern by the early 1400s — the last certain written record is a wedding at Hvalsey church in 1408. But economics set the fragility rather than necessarily striking the final blow: relations with the Inuit, cultural rigidity about farming methods, and simple choices all played parts historians still debate. The safe conclusion is layered: a colony that marginal can only persist while its trade pays for its lifeline, and when the arithmetic failed, there was no reserve left for bad luck.
In 1856 two Mormon handcart companies were caught by winter in Wyoming, with terrible loss of life. Why were they travelling so late in the year?

A chain of delays consumed the same margin that killed the Donner Party a decade earlier. The handcart scheme was an economy measure: emigrants too poor for wagons and oxen would pull their belongings some 2,100 kilometres from Iowa City to Salt Lake City in wooden carts, and the system worked for the companies that left on schedule. The Willie and Martin companies, though, were delayed at every stage — late arrival from England, carts built of green wood that kept breaking, outfitting bottlenecks in Iowa — and they started west in July despite warnings, reasoning that earlier companies had made it. October snows caught them in Wyoming, under-provisioned and with carts failing; rescue wagons sent out from Salt Lake City, once the alarm arrived, saved most of them, but on the order of two hundred emigrants died across the two companies. The structural lesson is identical to the Donner case and the Oregon Trail's spring window: overland migration had a closing date set by mountain weather, and every delay upstream was spent from the same account.
On the Santa Fe Trail, traders could choose a shorter route or a safer route. What was the trade-off?

Water against distance. The main route swung north to the Arkansas River and followed water most of the way, at the price of extra days. The Cimarron Cutoff saved several days' travel but crossed a stretch of high plains with almost no dependable water — a jornada where wagon trains depended on a few known springs, carried what water they could in barrels, crossed in the cool hours, and sometimes lost draft animals wholesale when a spring was dry or a train misjudged the distance. Freight economics priced the gamble precisely: days saved were profit, but a train that lost its mules lost everything. Most trains took the cutoff in good seasons and thought hard in dry ones. It is the desert version of a universal logistics problem — the shortest line on the map is measured in kilometres, but caravans and convoys pay in water, forage, and fuel, and by that accounting the 'long' route along the river was often the cheaper road.
Why do so many Great Plains towns sit at suspiciously regular intervals along the railways?

Because settlement beaded itself along the line at the spacing of a wagon haul. A farm family would haul grain by wagon roughly one day's round trip — on the order of fifteen to twenty kilometres — so grain elevators and the towns that grew around them were platted at intervals of about that distance along the track. The railroads, which received huge land grants, had every incentive to plat the towns themselves: they sold the lots, sold the surrounding farmland, and collected the freight on everything the town produced and consumed. Steam locomotives' need for water stops reinforced the rhythm of sidings and section points. The result is a settlement pattern you can still read from the air: towns strung like beads, each once the market for a wagon-sized hinterland. Where a railroad bypassed an existing settlement, the town often picked up and moved to the line, or died where it stood. On the plains, the railway didn't serve the map of settlement — it authored it.
Why did the United States care so much about a canal through Panama that it helped Panama become independent to build one?

The argument had been made in 1898 by a single warship. During the Spanish-American War, the battleship Oregon, stationed on the Pacific coast, was needed in the Caribbean — and had to steam all the way around South America, a voyage of some 23,000 kilometres taking about two months, while the war it was rushing to join was already being fought. The canal, opened in 1914, cut the sea journey between New York and San Francisco from roughly 22,500 kilometres around Cape Horn to about 9,500 through Panama — well over half the distance deleted. For a country with two coasts and one navy, that meant the fleet could concentrate in either ocean in weeks instead of months, and for commerce it re-sorted trade routes across the whole hemisphere. When Colombia balked at the treaty terms, the United States backed Panama's secession and signed with the new republic instead. The Oregon's dash is the cleanest illustration of how a single logistics fact — the sailing time between your own coasts — can bend diplomacy, sovereignty, and engineering into line behind it.
Leningrad survived a siege of nearly 900 days. What physically kept it alive?

A lake, a calendar, and a thickness of ice. Encircled from September 1941, the city's only supply route ran across Lake Ladoga — by barge in open water, and in winter over the ice road remembered as the Road of Life. Trucks could cross once the ice reached roughly twenty centimetres, but loads had to be kept light, vehicles spaced out, and the route shifted as the ice shifted; too early or too greedy and trucks went through. Across the siege, on the order of a million and a half tons of supplies came in over Ladoga and well over a million people were evacuated out, much of it over that ice. At the worst point, in November–December 1941, the bread ration for dependents fell to 125 grams a day — a figure that is the siege reduced to arithmetic: calories in, against mouths, against days. The city held because the ice held, because drivers kept crossing under shellfire as it thinned in spring, and because the margin, though starvation-thin, never quite reached zero. A siege is a race between two clocks, and Leningrad's was wound by a frozen lake.
Could the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad have been supplied by air, as Göring promised?

The arithmetic said no from the first day, and the arithmetic was available to everyone. The encircled army — roughly a quarter of a million men — needed, by the most austere staff estimate, around 300 tons of food, fuel, and ammunition a day merely to subsist; fuller estimates ran far higher. Göring promised the Luftwaffe could deliver it. In practice, weather, Soviet fighters and flak, long distances from the airfields outside the pocket, and a transport fleet already worn thin delivered well under a hundred tons a day on average — and cost nearly five hundred aircraft doing it. Every shortfall was cumulative: horses were eaten, then rations cut, then the men's strength to hold the perimeter went. When the last airfield inside the pocket, Pitomnik, fell in January 1943, deliveries dropped to parachute drops and the equation reached zero; the army surrendered within weeks. Stalingrad is the definitive case study in air supply: an airlift is a promise denominated in tons per day, and it should be audited like one — aircraft, weather, distance, and enemy action all take their percentage before the first ration lands.
At Alesia in 52 BC, Caesar besieged Vercingetorix — and then built a second wall facing outward. What was going on?

Caesar had calculated that he would be besieged himself, and built for both directions. His army surrounded Alesia, where Vercingetorix and a large Gallic force were trapped, with a ring of fortifications facing inward — on the order of eighteen kilometres of ditch, rampart, and traps. Knowing a Gallic relief army was coming, he then built a second, longer ring facing outward, and sat his army between the two, living off stockpiled supplies. The siege thus became two food clocks racing: inside Alesia, the Gauls' stores ran down until they expelled their non-combatants — the local Mandubii, women and children — hoping Caesar would let them through or feed them; Caesar refused, and they starved between the lines, a decision his own account records without flinching. When the relief army arrived, the Romans had to fight on both walls at once, and nearly broke — but the relief failed, and Alesia's clock ran out first. Alesia is siegecraft as pure logistics: walls in both directions, and victory to the side whose granary emptied last.
Why did the Great Siege of Malta in 1565 come down to a race against a relief fleet from Sicily?

Because both sides were besieging each other's supply lines. The Ottoman expedition — tens of thousands of men — had crossed the sea to Malta and lived from its fleet and from Tripoli, while the Knights of St John and the Maltese, a few thousand defenders, held the harbour forts at the island's heart. The Ottomans could not easily storm the position, and every week of summer cost them men to dysentery in their camps and consumed the campaigning season; the defenders, short of everything, needed relief from Sicily — only about ninety kilometres away — before their food, powder, and strength ran out. So the siege's real timetable was written in two places at once: the rate of Ottoman sickness and supply, and the Spanish viceroy's agonizingly slow assembly of a relief force. When the relief finally landed in September, the exhausted Ottomans withdrew. Malta shows the siege's hidden structure: the fortress is only the visible contest. The decisive one is between two logistical clocks, and the shorter supply line usually owns the faster clock.
Tyre was an island fortress that had never been taken. How did Alexander the Great capture it in 332 BC?

By abolishing the island. Tyre stood about half a kilometre to a kilometre offshore, ringed by walls that ancient sources claim rose as high as 45 metres on the seaward side, and supplied and relieved by sea — impregnable to a king who, at that moment, had no fleet worth the name. Alexander's answer was civil engineering as siegecraft: his men demolished the old mainland city and tipped it into the strait, building a stone mole across to the island, widening it under fire from Tyrian ships and sorties until siege towers and rams could reach the walls. Meanwhile the naval balance flipped — Phoenician and Cypriot squadrons defected to Alexander and blockaded Tyre's harbours, converting his mole from a causeway under attack into the landward side of a complete investment. After seven months the city was stormed. The epilogue is written in geography: silt accumulated around the mole until island and mainland fused. Modern Tyre is a peninsula because a siege train needed a road — logistics permanently edited the coastline.
The siege of Acre (1189–91) lasted two years, which seems absurdly long. Why couldn't either side finish it?

Because it was a double siege, and both halves were fed just well enough to continue. The Crusader army besieging Acre was itself confronted by Saladin's field army in the hills behind it, so the besiegers lived in a fortified camp, starving and diseased in the winters, but kept alive by the one artery Saladin could not cut: the sea. Italian and northern fleets ferried in food, money, and reinforcements — costly, seasonal, but sufficient. Saladin's army, living off the interior, could harass and blockade but could not storm the Crusader camp or starve it while ships kept arriving. Inside Acre, the garrison was resupplied by sea in its turn whenever Muslim ships ran the blockade. The deadlock broke when the balance of delivery tipped: Richard I of England arrived by sea in June 1191 with money, siege engines, and supplies, the Crusader camp's strength surged, and Acre's own food arithmetic finally ran out — the garrison surrendered that July. Two years of siege was not indecision. It was two supply systems, one maritime and one terrestrial, grinding against each other at nearly equal rates until money and shipping changed the rate.
How did besieged Paris communicate with the outside world in 1870–71 — and why couldn't that save it?

By balloon and pigeon, in a triumph of ingenuity over the wrong half of the problem. Encircled by Prussian armies from September 1870, Paris — a city of about two million — sent out dozens of balloons, sixty-six by the usual count, carrying mail and passengers over the siege lines on the wind; replies came back by carrier pigeon bearing microfilmed dispatches, thousands of messages shrunk onto tiny films. Communication, in other words, was solved. Supply was not: nothing that flew could carry food in meaningful tonnage, and a modern capital eats its stored food in weeks. Parisians consumed the city's horses, then the famous menus of cats, dogs, rats, and zoo animals, while bread quality and quantity sank on a calculable schedule. The armistice of January 1871 was signed, essentially, when the flour did. Paris is the limiting case of siege arithmetic: a pre-modern fortress stored food for a garrison; a modern metropolis is a warehouse with two million mouths and a burn rate no balloon can dent. Information got out. Calories couldn't get in. The calories decided.
What happened at Kut in 1916, and why is it remembered as a humiliation?

A British-Indian force of about thirteen thousand fighting men, under General Townshend, retreated into Kut-al-Amara on the Tigris in December 1915 and was besieged there by the Ottomans. Townshend had overestimated his food stocks — the arithmetic on which everything else depended — and rations were cut again and again as the months passed. Relief depended on the river: British forces fought their way up the Tigris at heavy cost and failed to break through, and a last attempt to run supplies in by the steamer Julnar ended with the ship captured. In April 1916, after 147 days, Townshend surrendered — one of the largest capitulations in British military history — and a large share of his men died in captivity on the marches and in the camps that followed. Kut's lesson is the besieger's oldest: a garrison is not a fixed asset but a consumption rate. Shut a force inside walls with finite food and the calendar becomes the enemy's artillery, firing every day without using a shell. Townshend chose a position his supply arithmetic could not defend, and the arithmetic collected.
Geography clearly mattered at Midway in 1942 — an island airfield in the middle of the Pacific. But is geography really why the US won?

Only partly, and this is the case to keep geographers honest. Midway's position mattered structurally: it was a fixed, unsinkable airfield within range of Hawaii that Japan needed to neutralize and the US could reinforce, and its loss or retention genuinely changed the local map. But the battle's outcome turned on information and accident, not terrain. American codebreakers had identified the target — famously confirming it by having Midway broadcast a report about a water problem, which Japanese traffic then repeated — so Nimitz ambushed the ambushers, positioning his carriers where Nagumo did not expect any. Japanese scouting then failed at the margin: one cruiser's floatplane, launched late, found the American fleet after the strike plans were set. Geography had dealt Japan the stronger hand — more carriers, a veteran air arm, the initiative — and a purely geographic reading predicts a Japanese victory. What overrode the map was a broken code, a ruse about drinking water, and a delayed scout plane. Geography loads the dice in war; at Midway, intelligence picked them up and threw them.
Hannibal won battle after battle in Italy for fifteen years, including Cannae. If his generalship and logistics were that good, why did he lose the war?

Because the things he lacked were not things a battlefield genius can improvise. Hannibal's logistics of movement were brilliant — over the Alps, then fifteen years living off Italy — and Cannae in 216 BC annihilated a Roman army. But Rome's war-making depth was political and demographic, and it held: most of Rome's Italian allies did not defect even after Cannae, so Hannibal could never convert victories into a new Italy; Rome refused battle on his terms for years under Fabius's delaying strategy and refused all negotiation; and Hannibal never received the siege train or the steady reinforcements needed to take Rome itself or hold the ports through which Carthage might supply him. His brother Hasdrubal's reinforcing army was destroyed at the Metaurus in 207 BC trying to reach him. In the end Hannibal was recalled to defend Carthage and beaten at Zama by Scipio — with Numidian cavalry that had changed sides. The honest framing: Hannibal solved the geography of getting there and the tactics of winning there. The war was decided one level up, by alliance systems, manpower reserves, and sea control — the deep logistics of states, which no march over mountains could outflank.
Why did the Mongols suddenly withdraw from Hungary in 1242, after conquering everything in their path?

Nobody knows for certain, and the competing explanations are a perfect lesson in not letting a tidy story outrun the evidence. The traditional account is political: the Great Khan Ögedei died in December 1241, and Mongol princes and armies were recalled toward Mongolia for the succession — after which the Mongols never returned to Hungary in force. Revisionist historians argue the geography itself pushed them out: the Hungarian plain is the westernmost tongue of the Eurasian steppe, and it may simply have been too small to graze the enormous horse herds — several remounts per trooper, across the whole army — that Mongol warfare required; an unusually wet period flooding the plain would have worsened the forage problem, and Hungary's stone castles, unlike its towns, had largely held, denying the Mongols secure bases. Both cases have serious evidence and serious defenders. The honest answer is that succession politics, pasture limits, weather, and fortification all plausibly contributed, and the sources don't let us crown one. Beware any single-cause explanation of a withdrawal, geographic or otherwise — empires usually leave for a committee of reasons.
The Spanish Armada was beaten by the 'Protestant wind,' wasn't it? How much did weather really contribute in 1588?

Weather did the final execution, but the campaign had already failed on structure before the storms took over. The Armada's mission contained a logistical impossibility: it had to rendezvous off Flanders with the Duke of Parma's invasion army, whose flat-bottomed barges needed days to embark troops and could only sail from shallow ports blockaded by Dutch flyboats — while the Armada's deep-draft warships could not enter those shallows to protect them. The link-up never happened. Then English fireships broke the Armada's defensive crescent at Calais, English gunnery — longer-ranged and faster-firing than Spanish boarding tactics — mauled it at Gravelines, and the wind forced the only way home: north around Scotland and Ireland, where autumn storms wrecked ship after ship. In the end roughly a third of the fleet was lost, more to weather and wreck than to English shot. The tidy version — God blew and they were scattered — hides the mechanism: geography and draft depths had already made the plan nearly unworkable, and the weather merely collected on a debt the plan had incurred.
Harold Godwinson's army had just marched the length of England twice in three weeks when it fought at Hastings in 1066. Did exhaustion lose the battle?

It contributed to the conditions, but claiming it lost the battle overstates what fatigue can explain. The marches were real logistics: Harold rushed some 300 kilometres north to destroy a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then, hearing of William's landing, force-marched back south, reaching the Hastings area by 13 October with an army missing some of its strength — the northern earls' contingents never joined him, and many of his men were footsore levies gathered on the road. Yet the tired army then held a strong hilltop position against Norman attacks for most of a day, which is not what collapse from exhaustion looks like. The shield wall broke late, through Norman feigned retreats that drew men downhill out of formation, and Harold's death late in the battle removed the army's centre of will. A fully rested, fully assembled English army might have won; it might also have been drawn off the same hill by the same tactic. Geography and marching explain the army Harold had. Tactics and a king's death explain the result he got.
Waterloo is often explained by mud and the ridge. Is that explanation sufficient?

No — the mud and the ridge were the same for everyone, and the battle turned on what men decided to do with them. The night's rain genuinely mattered: Napoleon delayed his opening until late morning so the ground would dry enough for artillery and manoeuvre, and those hours were irreplaceable. Wellington's ridge genuinely mattered: his reverse-slope defence sheltered his infantry and anchored the position he had chosen in advance. But the decisive fact is that the Prussian army, beaten two days earlier at Ligny, marched to the sound of the guns across roughly fifteen kilometres of the same mud — Blücher and Gneisenau choosing the sodden direct route and a promise kept to Wellington — and began arriving on Napoleon's flank in the late afternoon. Grouchy's French force, with the other half of the equation, did not march to the sound of anything. Geography set the stage with perfect impartiality: one ridge, one quagmire, one distance. The result came from which commanders treated those facts as constraints to plan around and which treated them as excuses to wait. That is the proper limit of geographic explanation — it deals the cards; it does not play the hand.
